pass_a_gloss: [...] the blessed David: I said in my being beside myself: every man a liar. And the same account would come to be both about God and about us and in the case of all the others; such as in the case of the righteousness, for someone would say, and not outside reason: let God become righteous, and every man unrighteous. But if our unrighteousness commends God's righteousness. The pretext of such a slander has come about from here: after the going back up from Babylon the sons of Israel, having been ordered by Cyrus to build up again the shrine and to fulfil vows and to bring sacrifices, became slack, making the pretext of poverty and the distress from the captivity; on this account they were being brought to their senses by proportionate disciplines, barrenness of fruits and lacks of rains; and being vexed at such blows, they were calling blessed the foreigners and those not serving God, as passing life in cheerfulness, and kept saying that those were better than themselves; and indeed Malachi the prophet kept saying to them: You weighed down upon me your words, says the Lord, and you said: In what did we speak against you? You said, he says: Vain is the one serving God, and what more, that we guarded his guardings, and because we went as suppliants before the face of the Lord Almighty? And now we call strangers blessed, and they are built up, doing lawless things; they stood against God and were saved. These things those fearing the Lord spoke against, each toward his neighbour; and the Lord paid attention and listened. For the sake of this cause, he says, some were supposing the Jews to say: Let us do the bad things, so that the good things may come; and saying the judgment is just, either of those attaching those things to Jews, or rather of those daring to say: Let us do the bad things, so that the good things may come. But now apart from law righteousness of God has been made visible. I know that it has been written about some, that they were both righteous, going in the commandments and ordinances of Christ blameless; and the blessed Paul too said that he himself according to the righteousness in law had become blameless. But the one blameless in these things has not yet done the things through which he will be brilliant and sung of; and indeed the blessed Paul himself said again that he was regarding all the things in law as loss and was counting them equal to refuse, and would seek again the surpassing of the knowledge of Christ. And again the law condemns those transgressing; for this reason elsewhere he says: For if to the service of the condemnation [there was] glory, much more abounds the service of the righteousness in glory; and there being very much commandment in it, it is in some way all necessity that even the exact guardian of law trip in some things and be set down a transgressor of law. And that it is truly burdensome, the divinely spoken disciples have clearly agreed; for they kept saying: Now then why do you test God, to lay a yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were strong enough to carry?
pass_b_english: …the blessed David: “I said in my alarm, ‘Every man is a liar’” (Psalm 116:11). The same reasoning would apply to God and to us in all other matters too; for example, in the matter of righteousness. For one could say, and not unreasonably, “Let God be righteous, and every man unrighteous.”

“But if our unrighteousness shows the righteousness of God” (Romans 3:5). The occasion for this slander arose in this way. After the return from Babylon, the sons of Israel, ordered by Cyrus to rebuild the temple, to pay their vows and to offer sacrifices, grew slack, pleading poverty and the hardship left by the captivity. For this they were corrected by measured chastisements: failed harvests and lack of rain (Haggai 1:9–11). Chafing at such blows, they called the foreigners and those who did not serve God happy, as living in good cheer, and said that those people were better off than they were. And so the prophet Malachi said to them: “You have made your words heavy against me, says the Lord. And you said, ‘How have we spoken against you?’ You said,” he says, “‘It is vain to serve God. What more have we gained because we kept his charges, and because we walked as suppliants before the Lord Almighty? And now we call strangers happy, and those who do lawless deeds are built up; they opposed God and were saved.’ This is how those who feared the Lord spoke against him, each to his neighbor; and the Lord gave heed and heard” (Malachi 3:13–16).

For this reason, he says, some thought that the Jews were saying, “Let us do evil so that good may come” (Romans 3:8). But when he says that their condemnation is just, he means those who pinned those words on the Jews, or rather those who dared to say, “Let us do evil so that good may come.”

“But now the righteousness of God has been made manifest apart from the law” (Romans 3:21). I know that it is written of certain people that “they were both righteous, walking blameless in the commandments and ordinances of Christ” (Luke 1:6); and the blessed Paul too said that he himself had become “blameless as to the righteousness that is in the law” (Philippians 3:6). But one who is blameless in these things has not yet done the deeds that will make him illustrious and renowned. Indeed, the blessed Paul himself said again that he counted everything in the law as loss and reckoned it as so much refuse, and that he would seek instead “the surpassing excellence of the knowledge of Christ” (Philippians 3:7–8).

Again, the law condemns those who transgress; that is why he says elsewhere, “For if there was glory in the ministry of condemnation, much more does the ministry of righteousness abound in glory” (2 Corinthians 3:9). And since the law contains a great many commandments, even the careful keeper of the law must surely stumble in some of them and become a transgressor of the law. The inspired disciples plainly admitted that it is truly burdensome, for they said: “Now therefore, why are you putting God to the test by placing on the neck of the disciples a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?” (Acts 15:10).

revisions.summary: Pass A, lemmas, choices and bible_refs rebuilt from the Greek to match the reviewed English; pass_b_english is the current English.

review_notes: Old draft had many wrong senses: it applied 'every man is a liar' to God; cited Romans 3:4 for Cyril's own analogy 'Let God be righteous'; said the Israelites 'remained unshakeable' when they chafed (ἀσχάλλοντες); mistranslated συμμέτροις παιδείαις as 'moderate educations' (now 'measured chastisements'); cited Malachi 2:4 and 3:14-15 for a single quotation of Malachi 3:13-16 LXX and detached its last lines as narrative; reversed agency at Romans 3:8 ('some Jews were inclined to say' where Greek has 'some thought the Jews said'); rendered λαμπρὸς καὶ ἀοίδιμος as 'without reproach'; turned πλείστης ἐντολῆς ('very many commandments') into 'a greater commandment'; and lacked citations for Psalm 116:11 (LXX 115:2), Luke 1:6, Philippians 3:6-8. Luke 1:6 kept as the source reads it ('of Christ'; the Gospel has 'of the Lord'). Opening ellipsis continues u01-open. Old translator_notes ('guardrails', 'vain one', OCR remarks) describe the discarded draft and should be dropped.
Opens mid-sentence, continuing the end of u01-open.
Malachi 3:13–16 is one quotation from the Septuagint, kept together.
Romans 3:8: some thought that the Jews were saying 'Let us do evil so that good may come'; the saying is not put in the mouth of the Jews themselves.
Luke 1:6 is kept as the source reads it ('of Christ'); the Gospel has 'of the Lord'.
